questions.explanation: A concentrated constitutional court decides the constitutional question and its holding binds later courts, which is the point of centralising review. Advisory opinions carry no such force, discretion describes diffuse review, and only a formal amendment or some comparable device displaces a settled holding.
questions.hint: Ask what a later court is free to do with the first ruling.

questions.explanation: Packing works by adding judges or easing the conditions for the court to act, which changes the institution before any case is decided, so opponents call it an attempt to tilt outcomes. Changing a docket, an appointment procedure, or publication rules leaves the court's existing composition and authority intact.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change touches the institution or one case.

answer.exemplar: The timing target counts minutes to a decision, not whether the decision was right, so staff can hit it by deciding quickly and referring hard cases onward, which then shows up later as appeals rather than as a miss on the clock. A better set pairs speed with a quality measure such as the share of decisions upheld on appeal, and with an outcome measure like unresolved complaints, so a target cannot be met by moving work rather than finishing it.

questions.explanation: A strong answer distinguishes what an indicator counts from what citizens experience, shows how a queue metric can be met by deferring hard cases, and then specifies a paired quality or appeal measure. Stopping at the speed statistic repeats the regulator's own blind spot instead of naming the missing dimension.
questions.hint: Ask what the indicator counts rather than what citizens experience.
